name: Seismic Strengthening
plain: How can existing masonry-infilled structures be strengthened against seismic demand without adding unnecessary weight or complexity?
technical: Doctoral research investigated the confinement of masonry infills in RC moment-resisting frames using cost-effective skin reinforcement, supported by experimental, analytical and numerical studies.
problem: In much of South India, framed buildings are filled with unreinforced masonry. The frame is designed; the infill is not. Under cyclic loading the infill attracts force it was never detailed to carry, and can fail out-of-plane even where the frame survives.
approach: Panels were tested under cyclic load with skin reinforcement — wire mesh applied to the wall face and anchored into the frame — and compared against unreinforced and confined alternatives. Results were then generalised analytically into an equivalent-strut width that designers can use, and checked numerically.
contribution: A strengthening method that uses commonly available mesh and mortar, adds little mass, and can be applied to a building that already exists; plus an equivalent-strut formulation for wire-meshed infill under dynamic loading.
next: The same question — how to restrain masonry economically — carries into the granted GI-netting patent at the beam–column joint, and into the proposed additive printing work for masonry.

name: Masonry Structures
plain: What does masonry actually do inside a concrete frame, and how should that be represented in design?
technical: Experimental and analytical study of confined masonry, infill–frame interaction, latex-modified and conventional mortars, and alternate wall materials under cyclic load.
problem: Masonry is usually treated as non-structural, then behaves structurally. Its stiffness changes how the whole frame responds.
approach: Wall panels and portal frames tested under cyclic loading, with variations in mortar, confinement and reinforcement; strut-based idealisations fitted to the measured behaviour.
contribution: Measured performance for several practical wall build-ups, including latex-modified mortar and natural-fibre brick, and strut-width estimates for meshed infill.
next: Feeds the materials work on alternate wall systems and the additive-printing proposal for masonry.

name: 3D Concrete Printing
plain: Concrete can now be printed rather than cast — but printed concrete still has to be reinforced. How do you do both at once?
technical: Work on printable cementitious mixes, structural build-up and set control, and on print-head and multi-arm systems that integrate reinforcement during deposition.
problem: Extrusion printing asks contradictory things of a mix: it must pump and flow, then immediately hold its own shape under the next layer. Separately, reinforcement — the thing that makes concrete structural — is still usually placed by hand, which gives back the time automation saved.
approach: On the material side, nano-silica and accelerator systems were studied as structural build-up agents, and alkaline-activated compositions developed for extrusion. On the machine side, a print head for reinforced elements and the TriFusion multi-arm system were developed and filed.
contribution: Two published patent applications on the material and the print head, a filed system-level application, and a funded prototype currently being built under the Karunya Short-Term Research Grant.
next: Building and structurally validating the multi-arm prototype, including a 2 ft × 2 ft working model.

name: Additive Manufacturing in Construction
plain: What changes when a building component is manufactured additively instead of formed in a mould?
technical: Review and experimental work on additive manufacturing techniques in construction, printable material behaviour and reinforcement integration.
problem: Additive methods are mature in other industries and still immature in construction, where scale, ambient conditions and structural codes all differ.
approach: A review of the available techniques and their constraints, followed by doctoral supervision and funded prototype work on printable materials and multi-arm deposition.
contribution: A reviewed account of the technique landscape, a completed doctorate in printable cementitious materials, and filed intellectual property.
next: Extending the method from cementitious elements toward masonry systems.

name: AI and Machine Learning in Construction
plain: Construction generates a great deal of data — images of cracks, fabrication records, material consumption. Can that data be used to predict and to inspect?
technical: Deep-learning crack characterisation in buildings; probabilistic grouping and random-forest regression for consumables forecasting in pre-engineered building fabrication.
problem: Inspection is manual and inconsistent; fabrication planning relies on estimates that are hard to hold to.
approach: Convolutional models trained to characterise cracks from building imagery; regression and grouping models applied to real pre-engineered-building fabrication records.
contribution: Published methods for both, with a doctoral scholar currently working on classification and forecasting of fabrication dynamics in pre-engineered buildings.
next: Linking prediction to the monitoring work, so that a model informs inspection rather than only reporting on it.

name: BIM and Scan-to-BIM
plain: Most existing buildings have no usable digital model. Can one be built from a scan of the building as it actually stands?
technical: Techniques, mapping strategies and building life-cycle applications for integrating scan data into BIM.
problem: Drawings, where they exist, record what was intended rather than what was built. Assessment and retrofit both need the second.
approach: A structured review of capture techniques and of the mapping strategies that turn point-cloud data into structured model elements, organised by life-cycle stage.
contribution: A consolidated account of where scan-to-BIM currently works and where it does not.
next: Connecting the captured model to structural monitoring, so that the model carries condition and not only geometry.

name: Structural Health Monitoring
plain: How do we know whether a structure is still sound, without taking it apart?
technical: Damage characterisation from building imagery and scan data, alongside damping and response studies on framed structures.
problem: Condition assessment is periodic, subjective and often too late.
approach: Imaging and deep learning for crack characterisation; scan-derived models as a geometric baseline; experimental work on damping devices and structural response.
contribution: Published crack-characterisation methods and a body of measured response data for damped frames.
next: Bringing the monitoring signal and the digital model together.

name: Structural Engineering
plain: How do framed structures carry load, and how can their response be controlled?
technical: Composite and encased frames under cyclic load, buckling-restrained braces, fluid-viscous and magnetorheological dampers, topology optimisation, and code-comparison studies.
problem: Controlling the response of a frame — rather than only sizing it — is what determines how it performs in an earthquake or a wind event.
approach: Experimental cyclic testing of composite and steel-encased frames, and analytical and numerical study of bracing, damping devices and optimisation methods.
contribution: A sustained experimental record on composite frames and damping systems, including comparative work at two damper scales.
next: Applying the same response-control thinking to printed and hybrid structural elements.

name: Construction Materials
plain: Can a material be made to perform better, cost less, or use less of what is scarce?
technical: Toughness enhancement in cement mortar, latex-modified mortar, self-compacting concrete with copper slag and fly ash, sea sand as partial replacement for M-sand, natural-fibre brick, metakaolin-blended blocks and soil stabilisation.
problem: River sand and clinker are both constrained; performance requirements are not.
approach: Systematic mix-level experimental programmes, each substituting one constituent and measuring the consequence.
contribution: A long series of characterised alternatives, several of which feed directly into the printable-material and masonry work.
next: Carrying the substitution logic into printable mixes, where rheology constrains the choice further.

name: Sustainable Construction
plain: Can construction use waste streams and lower-clinker binders without giving up structural performance?
technical: Industrial by-products as aggregate and binder replacement, alkaline-activated compositions, bamboo reinforcement and agricultural-waste-based blocks.
problem: Cement production and sand extraction both carry costs that the structure itself never records.
approach: Replacement studies across concrete and masonry, evaluated on strength and workability rather than on intent.
contribution: Measured performance for copper slag, fly ash, metakaolin-blended palm kernel shell, sea sand and bamboo in specific applications.
next: Alkaline-activated printable compositions, where the sustainability case and the printability case coincide.

name: Mixed Reality in Construction
plain: Can a model be read on site, against the structure itself, rather than on a drawing?
technical: An active research interest in mixed-reality methods for construction, developing alongside the scan-to-BIM work.
problem: The gap between a digital model and the site is still crossed by paper.
approach: Currently a direction of inquiry rather than a completed programme; it follows naturally from the scan-to-BIM results.
next: Connecting captured models to on-site visualisation.

name: Environment and Health
plain: What is in the air, and what does it do to the people breathing it?
technical: Collaborative work on bioaerosol characterisation and sampling, rural airborne microorganisms and antimicrobial resistance, and climatic determinants of public-health incidence.
problem: Air quality and the built environment are not separate problems, but they are usually studied separately.
approach: Co-authored interdisciplinary studies with environmental science and public-health colleagues.
contribution: Contributing author on several studies, including a widely cited review of bioaerosol characterisation and sampling.
next: Continued collaboration across the environment and built-environment boundary.
